title: Design a multi-channel notification system
prompt: A product team needs to fan out notifications across push, email, and SMS. The dominant forcing constraint is fan-out under bursty load: a single event (a sale, a breaking-news alert) can trigger millions of sends to slow, flaky third-party providers. Senders must be decoupled from the request path so a spike or a provider outage never blocks ingestion. Draw how a notification request enters the system, gets durably buffered, and is delivered asynchronously across channels — including where templates and per-message delivery status live, and how you keep duplicate/over-rate sends in check.

criteria.label: Notification requests originate from a client or upstream caller
criteria.metWhy: Good — the flow starts from a real caller submitting notification requests.
criteria.why: Add a User/Client component to represent the upstream service or app that triggers notifications.

criteria.label: An ingestion service or API accepts incoming notification requests
criteria.metWhy: Good — there is a compute tier that validates and accepts notification requests.
criteria.why: Add an API Gateway or Server/Service to receive and validate incoming notification requests before they are processed.

criteria.label: A queue decouples ingestion from delivery (the core piece)
criteria.metWhy: Excellent — a queue absorbs bursts and decouples fast ingestion from slow, flaky provider sends.
criteria.why: Fan-out is the forcing constraint here. Add a Queue so a burst or a provider outage never blocks request ingestion.

criteria.label: Ingestion service writes requests onto the queue
criteria.metWhy: Good — accepted requests are enqueued instead of being sent inline on the request path.
criteria.why: Connect your ingestion API/Service to the Queue so requests are buffered durably rather than sent synchronously.

criteria.label: A worker/sender tier drains the queue and delivers to channels
criteria.metWhy: Good — dedicated workers pull from the queue and call push/email/SMS providers.
criteria.why: Add a Server/Service acting as a worker that consumes the queue and dispatches to the notification channels.

criteria.label: Workers consume from the queue
criteria.metWhy: Good — the delivery path reads from the queue, so it can retry independently of ingestion.
criteria.why: Connect your worker/sender Server to the Queue so delivery is driven asynchronously and can retry on provider failures.

criteria.label: A database holds templates and per-message delivery status
criteria.metWhy: Durable store of record for templates, preferences, and delivery/retry status.
criteria.why: Add a Database to persist message templates, user preferences, and per-message delivery status for retries and auditing.

criteria.label: The service or worker reads/writes the database
criteria.metWhy: Good — the compute tier persists templates and delivery status in the datastore.
criteria.why: Connect your Service/API or worker to the Database so templates and delivery status are actually read and updated.

criteria.label: A cache supports rate-limiting and dedupe of sends
criteria.metWhy: Good — a fast in-memory store enforces per-user rate limits and suppresses duplicate sends.
criteria.why: Add a Cache to track rate-limit counters and idempotency/dedupe keys so users are not spammed with duplicate notifications.
